title: Detaining Families, Policing Pregnancy: Trump's Immigration Crackdown on Women and Children
authors: Abby Wheatley, Giovanna DeStefanis, Madeline Dyer
description:
Immediately following this order, more than 2,100 pregnant women were detained, many of whom were detained upwards of weeks or months.
It is a practice designed to detain whole families in immigration facilities while they await hearings.
… Pregnant women … require specialized healthcare, access to medical labs and high-quality ultrasounds that are not readily available in detention facilities.
Family detention allows the administration to get around the optics of separating families while ramping up immigrant detention and undermining the rights of families and children.
The Problem With Family Detention Family detention is not simply another anti-immigrant policy; it is anti-woman, anti-mother and anti-family.
text:
Trump’s renewed family detention policies and attacks on birthright citizenship are expanding a system that subjects immigrant mothers and children to incarceration, medical neglect and lasting harm.

On Aug. 6, just days after the Supreme Court struck down Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14160, which aimed to remove birthright citizenship for children of undocumented parents and temporary visitors, the president signed two new executive orders targeting birthright citizenship and so-called birth tourism.

The first order, “Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship,” aims to exclude babies born to employees working for foreign governments, among others.

The second order, “Ending Birth Tourism,” denies visas to women suspected of misrepresenting their reason for traveling to the U.S. in order to give birth on U.S. soil.

These executive orders are the administration’s latest attempt to police American identity, punish migrant women for entering the U.S. and ultimately regulate their reproduction. Beyond the issue of birthright citizenship, immigrant women and children continue to be targets of a hostile immigration system that seeks to control them through detention, family separation and deportation.

Trump’s efforts to criminalize and punish women, including mothers and pregnant women, have been expanding since his first term, when he signed Executive Order 13768, “Enhancing Public Safety in the Interior of the United States in 2017,” removing protections for pregnant women to allow for their frequent detention in immigration facilities. This EO ensured pregnant women could be held in detention centers, despite the fact that they require specialized healthcare, access to medical labs and high-quality ultrasounds that are not readily available in these facilities.

Immediately following this order, more than 2,100 pregnant women were detained, many of whom were detained upwards of weeks or months.

What Is Family Detention?

In 2018, Trump implemented a “zero tolerance” policy that resulted in the separation of more than 5,000 families and the incarceration of children as young as 4 months. These children were housed in abhorrent conditions and without basic amenities, including a blanket, toothbrush and something to eat. Images of children held behind chain-link fencing sparked public outrage on both sides of the political spectrum and the family separations eventually ended, though as of 2024 as many as 1,360 children still had not been reunited with their families.

Family detention differs from the earlier zero tolerance policy that resulted in children being separated from their parents, but it’s no less traumatic. It is a practice designed to detain whole families in immigration facilities while they await hearings.

While halted under Biden, many people don’t know that the Trump administration reinstated family detention in March 2025 and reopened two family detention centers in Texas: the Karnes Family Civil Detention Center in Karnes County, which can house 830 people, and the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, which has space for 2,400 people. Both the Karnes County and South Texas facilities are run by private companies: CoreCivic and GEO Group, respectively.

… Pregnant women … require specialized healthcare, access to medical labs and high-quality ultrasounds that are not readily available in detention facilities.

Family detention allows the administration to get around the optics of separating families while ramping up immigrant detention and undermining the rights of families and children. In fact, since 2025, “the number of families in detention centers has more than tripled,” according to a report by the Children’s Equity Center, “detaining children of all ages, starting in infancy.” These facilities function like civil detention centers or prisons and are unsuitable for stays of any duration.

In addition, minors are being held in residential centers much longer than the 20-day limit set by the Flores Agreement, a 1997 law which outlines basic standards of care for minors in immigration detention.

The Problem With Family Detention

Family detention is not simply another anti-immigrant policy; it is anti-woman, anti-mother and anti-family.

Family residential facilities make it possible to mass criminalize and incarcerate women, mothers and children by creating supposedly, but not actually, appropriate bed space for families to be detained together. Still, the poor conditions of family residential facilities are well-documented by human rights groups and policy centers, including Human Rights First and the Children’s Equity Project at Arizona State University.

Simply being detained presents a medical risk as families experience interrupted medical treatment, inadequate access to health screenings and long-lasting physical and psychological problems. In a recent report, Human Rights First found that “children and their parents have limited access to clean water, nutritious food, sleep, personal hygiene, privacy, or clean or appropriate clothing.”

There is also evidence that migrant women in detention face increased abuse, including sexual assault by officers who have authority over them. Between 2010 and 2016, approximately 33,000 allegations of abuse were received by the DHS Office of Inspector General.

“The sexual abuse of immigration detainees,” according to the ACLU, “is not an isolated problem limited to a few rogue facilities or to a handful of bad-apple government contractors who staff some of the nation’s immigration jails.”

The vulnerability of women is heightened when they are caring for small children, pregnant or postpartum. These instances of neglect and mistreatment are not anomalies; they are integral to a migration management system that seeks to securitize the border by exacerbating the vulnerability of unauthorized migrants through punishments enacted on their bodies.

This pattern of neglect and abuse is not new.

In 2014, the Artesia Family Residential Center in New Mexico was closed down after reports of the center’s inhumane and “prison-like” conditions, inadequate health care and failure to meet child welfare guidelines.

The following year, Berks County Residential Center in Pennsylvania was charged with endangering the health and well-being of children. Despite this pattern of neglect, the center remained open until 2021 when the Biden administration halted the practice of family detention, transitioning all facilities away from long-term family detention.

Families Under Attack

The reinstatement of family residential facilities is part of a broader strategy to punish women for entering the country without authorization, for having children in the U.S. when they lack a legal status, for attempting to raise their children with the same rights and benefits of their peers. This was captured in an interview with Border Czar Tom Homan on CBS’ Face the Nation after three U.S. citizen children, including a 4-year-old with Stage 4 cancer, were deported along with their mothers to Honduras.

Homan justified the deportations by shifting responsibility from the administration to the women who “chose” to have children in the U.S. despite being undocumented, explaining:

“When you enter the country illegally, and you know you are here illegally, and you choose to have a U.S. citizen child, that’s on you. That’s not on this administration. If you choose to put your family in this position, that’s on them. But having a U.S. citizen child after you enter the country illegally, it’s not a get-out-of-jail-free card. It doesn’t make you immune from our laws.”

Even with the reinstatement of family detention, some families are still being separated. Twenty-five-year-old Ingrid Mejia, a farmworker from Guatemala, was detained for four months after driving without a license; her 3-year-old son was put into foster care.

Even after Mejia was released from ICE custody, her child, Eliazar, remained in foster care for several more months. Mejia had to participate in supervised visits and have her home inspected to ensure it was suitable for a child before she could regain custody of her son. Mejia’s case underscores the design of migration management to make the migration process painful, harmful, and incur lasting suffering.

Detaining pregnant mothers and families isn’t just about filling up detention centers to turn a profit or support tough-on-crime statistics. It is a way of penalizing pregnancy in immigrant communities to control and criminalize women’s bodies and their choices.

Though popular rhetoric focuses mainly on male migrants—presenting them as criminals, rapists and terrorists, using fear to stoke hatred of immigrants—the state deliberately mobilizes the resources to criminalize and incarcerate migrant women and children. This approach to border enforcement is inhumane and unjust as it relies on a series of corporeal punishments that deliberately exacerbate the vulnerability of women from the time they leave home until they enter immigration facilities in the U.S.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers may soon be outfitted with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks intended to gain compliance from combative individuals.

ICE plans to spend up to $20 million to purchase thousands of "conductive distraction and de-escalation devices" for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.

The devices are known as the G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky. They have been used in recent years by some jails and police departments.

Alexandra Lozano Kennedy — a former immigration attorney who made wide use of social media and Latino religious iconography to attract clientele — had offices across the U.S., including one in the city of Commerce in Southeast L.A.

Lozano Kennedy was licensed by the Washington State Bar Association, which enabled her to represent clients nationwide. In May, she resigned in lieu of discipline for misconduct and is permanently barred from practicing law in that state. As of June 2026, she is also suspended from practicing before the Department of Homeland Security, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services; immigration courts; and the Board of Immigration Appeals.

Lozano Kennedy, who had tens of thousands of clients, is accused of falsifying stories of trafficking and abuse without her clients’ knowledge, according to lawsuits and immigrant advocates.

At her office in Los Angeles County, clients were met with a large image of the Virgin of Guadalupe in the reception area, flanked by flowers and votive candles, much like a scene inside a local Catholic church. This holy image was also on business cards distributed at the locale. Lozano Kennedy’s use of this iconography as a business strategy harmed community members, said M. Lucero Ortiz, supervising attorney at Loyola Law School’s Immigrant Justice Clinic.

“A lot of them are questioning their own faith," Ortiz said.

“Her fraud really only had a shelf life of about five to six years, because that's how long these cases take to be processed,” Ortiz added.

The clinic she supervises is using social media to help Lozano Kennedy’s former clients navigate the fallout amid the Trump administration’s ongoing mass deportation campaign.

Lozano Kennedy billed herself as a miracle worker, Ortiz said. The work permits clients received as their applications made their way through the immigration process bolstered this belief.

"Clients would think: ‘Oh, my gosh! Everybody else told me that my case was too complex, but this woman got me a work permit in six to nine months,’" Ortiz said. “But what they didn't know is that, five years later, that case would be denied. And they would be in removal proceedings.”

What is Lozano Kennedy accused of?

According to the Washington State Bar Association, Lozano Kennedy's alleged misconduct includes:

directing staff to use a script that contained false and/or misleading information when communicating with prospective clients

filing applications for immigration benefits with USCIS when she knew the clients were ineligible for those benefits

using nonlawyers to perform legal functions on behalf of clients, and/or delegating legal functions to non-lawyer staff, such as performing client consultations and providing legal advice

Find a full list of her alleged misconduct here. Lozano Kennedy has denied any wrongdoing.

What do advocates recommend?

If you were represented by Lozano Kennedy and have petitions or applications pending before USCIS, the Immigrant Legal Resource Center and Loyola Law School’s Immigrant Justice Clinic have provided guidance for former clients. The latter recommends former clients take the following steps:

Open an account online at my.uscis.gov. This allows people with pending immigration cases to manage and track their status in real time, including filing applications, receiving digital notices, uploading evidence and communicating securely with USCIS officers.

Submit a change of address (USCIS Form AR-11) request. Be sure to file online and mail the request.

Cases with a receipt number starting with EAC should mail the request to the Vermont Service Center, USCIS Service Center Operations, Attn: Humanitarian Division, 38 River Rd., Essex Junction, VT 05479-0001.

Cases with a receipt number starting with LIN, should mail the request forms to the Nebraska Service Center, USCIS Service Center Operations, P.O. Box 87918, Lincoln, NE 68501-7918.

Send USCIS a revocation of legal representation letter expressing that you no longer want the attorney of record to represent you and that you will be representing yourself (pro se) while you hire another attorney.

Request a copy of your case file online at USCIS FOIA and through email from Luz Legal.

Check your case status at USCIS and immigration court.

Submit a request to the victims’ compensation fund with the Washington State Bar Association (WSBA).

After you receive a copy of your case file, consult a licensed and experienced attorney about the strategy in your case.

Ortiz, the supervising attorney at the clinic, stressed that these are all steps community members can take for themselves, without the help of an attorney. You can find details for each step here.

The Immigrant Justice Clinic also addressed these frequently asked questions:

Should all of Lozano Kennedy’s former clients withdraw their pending USCIS application?

No, if a pending case is withdrawn, it can lead to a notice to appear (NTA)/deportation process. Consult with a licensed and experienced attorney before making any decision regarding your case.

Are all former clients eligible to join the two pending civil lawsuits against Lozano Kennedy?

No, not all former clients will be able to join the pending lawsuits.

To learn more, former clients can share their contact information and a summary of their case online at https://lozanocivilaction.com/#register

In California, the statute of limitations for civil fraud claims is three years.

A civil lawsuit will not address or fix an individual’s pending immigration case.

For weeks, Lineage Logistics and the Los Angeles Fire Department have said ammonia — the hazardous material that’s key for industrial refrigerators — was quickly cleared from the warehouse fire zone. In the days after the fire, Lineage insisted that no measurable ammonia was detected in the area.

Now, community testing as well as data from Lineage and the Southern California Air Quality Management District show that elevated levels of ammonia were present in neighborhoods near the cold-storage warehouse weeks after the fire.

Though air regulators and Lineage note the levels didn’t meet the state threshold requiring action to protect public health, community groups say the findings are alarming. Meanwhile, federal regulators are seeking answers from Lineage to determine what air contaminants were released during the fire. Lineage did not respond to questions from Boyle Heights Beat.

An analysis published Aug. 5 by the Community and Environment Research Lab at UC Irvine and East Yard Communities for Environmental Justice found higher levels of ammonia in streets close to Lineage.

That includes Indiana Street near Union Pacific Avenue, where the highest ammonia levels — 4,300 parts per billion — were detected on Aug. 2, more than a month after the fire was extinguished, through handheld Aeroqual monitors that community scientists from East Yard have been using to sample the air.

Experts agree that’s many times higher than what’s considered typical, though the standard for ammonia levels in L.A.’s air varies.

UC Irvine and East Yard Communities for Environmental Justice classify 4 to 6 parts per billion as typical ammonia levels, a figure that’s also considered the baseline nationwide. To South Coast AQMD, typical background levels of ammonia in LA range up to 36 parts per billion.

The analysis by the Community and Environment Research Lab and UC Irvine also shows that higher-than-normal ammonia levels were also detected from a distance.

About a mile from Lineage, ammonia levels have reached 108 parts per billion, according to publicly available data retrieved from a stationary monitor that South Coast AQMD placed late July at Eastman Avenue Elementary School.

To Jill Johnston, associate professor of environmental and occupational health at UC Irvine, the findings not only show “very high” ammonia concentrations closer to the facility, but also how “these chemicals are traveling into the nearby neighborhoods.”

The recent data, Johnston said, suggests that the “big source of ammonia” is coming from the rotting food in Lineage. She also pointed to the ammonia used in the facility’s refrigeration system.

This analysis is just a snapshot of the potential air contaminants present near Lineage, said Johnston, an exposure scientist and environmental epidemiologist.

“In some ways it confirms what people have been experiencing for the last seven weeks … That they’re breathing poor air quality and subject to foul odors, and that we continue to see impacts on local air quality, even seven weeks into this process,” Johnston said.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, according to its website, said normal amounts of ammonia in the environment do not cause health effects in humans. However, the agency noted that exposure to high levels of ammonia “may hurt your skin, eyes, throat, and lungs and cause coughing and burns. Lung damage and death may occur after exposure to very high levels of ammonia.”

In a statement, South Coast AQMD said it has seen “some levels of ammonia” that were elevated above L.A. background levels at the Eastman Elementary monitor and from roaming ammonia measurements. South Coast AQMD declined to comment on the air sensors being used to take ammonia measurements.

However, the agency noted, California’s short-term health benchmark — the level of ammonia a person could inhale continuously for one hour without adverse health effects — is 4,500 parts per billion. Despite elevated levels recorded near Lineage, “they do not exceed the State’s short-term health standards,” South Coast AQMD said.

“We understand that the situation is dynamic and conditions are changing, particularly with the heat and the decomposing materials that have potential to offgas. We continue to monitor the situation closely,” the agency added.

These findings come on the heels of a letter that the Environmental Protection Agency sent to Lineage on Aug. 3, ordering the company to detail the “specific substances,” including “all air contaminants,” that were released during the time of the fire.

“The EPA is aware of a potential hazardous substance release event at the Lineage Logistics,” according to the letter. The agency did not state which substance and gave Lineage 14 days to provide them with the information.

Lineage, which has conducted air monitoring near the warehouse since June 23, said it has not identified chemical concentrations “above health-based action levels.” After saying on June 19 that it had not detected “measurable” amounts of ammonia, on Aug. 8, the company acknowledged on its website that “short-lasting ammonia detections” were observed at northern and eastern portions of the fire site. Lineage detected a peak of ammonia at 1,000 parts per billion.

Mark Lopez with East Yard Communities for Environmental Justice pushed back against the thresholds that air regulators are relying on to determine what’s safe and unsafe for residents.

“What we’re dealing with is not short-term exposure. We’re not dealing with one hour, two hours, six hours, eight hours. We’re dealing with a lot of folks who are there 24 hours. It’s inappropriate to use the lowest bar for protecting the community,” Lopez said. “They’re using a standard that’s inappropriate for the actual lived experiences of our community.”

Lopez said air regulators shouldn’t normalize the notion that “there’s always elevated levels of pollution in our communities ... What they’re seeing is not alarming, and we’re like, yeah, because you’re not alarmed by environmental racism, and that’s the problem,” Lopez said.

Los Angeles police defended the use of chemical agents against people protesting the federal immigration crackdown last year, the first time police had used the hazardous munitions since the 1970s.

Department administrators claimed at Tuesday’s Los Angeles Board of Police Commissioners meeting that the chemical agents were needed to control crowds and could be used again during major events in the future, such as the Super Bowl and the 2028 Olympics.

What LAPD said happened

Lt. Joseph Franzen and Commander Mario Mota discussed the use of tear gas, rubber bullets and other projectiles referenced in a 60-page LAPD report on the 2025 protests.

The report analyzed demonstrations, including ones at federal buildings in downtown L.A., between June 6 and June 17, 2025, which the department estimated peaked at about 20,000 participants.

Franzen, one of the report's authors, said it was intended to be a reflection on the department’s actions for future reference. The report does not detail injuries to members of the public and journalists, and does not include statements from them about what they experienced.

Commission President Rasha Gerges Shields asked the department to provide more information at a future meeting about injuries to members of the public and the amount and type of force used.

While the department said the chemical agents were needed to disperse crowds, their use has been the subject of ongoing debate. In January, a federal judge ordered the Police Department to stop using certain crowd-control weapons that posed risks to the public.

Shields said that order should have been included in the report.

Franzen and Mota said officers used chemical agents on June 8 and June 14, respectively, in response to large crowds that had grown unruly. They reported that officers had various items thrown at them.

Police Chief Jim McDonnell told the commissioners that most of the crowd exercised its First Amendment rights, but that a small portion of the crowd was “exceptionally violent.” He said he had never experienced that level of violence at a public gathering in his decades of police service.

Questions raised about the report

Several people at the Police Commission meeting contested the department’s account, saying chemical agents were used on journalists and members of the public they said were protesting peacefully or doing their jobs — with little warning.

The League of Women Voters of Greater Los Angeles wrote a letter in advance of the meeting, disagreeing with the characterization of the protests as "riots" in the report and urged better word choice.

“‘Rioting’ connotes serious violence,” wrote Carolina Goodman on behalf of the organization.

During her first meeting as a police commissioner, Heather Aubry asked Mota to clarify that whatever violence did occur was not sanctioned by the organizers of the various protests that took place over the study period.

L.A. resident Kayla Esmond joined a preplanned march that included children, seniors and disabled people hoping to protest federal immigration enforcement. She told the commissioners that people in the large crowd began yelling that police were preparing to use tear gas.

“There was no dispersal order,” Esmond told The LA Local. “Someone yelled that there were children present. They fired the canisters without any response or warning that we could hear.”

Mayor Karen Bass eventually issued a curfew for downtown L.A. on June 10. Franzen and Mota reported that 435 people were arrested during the protests. Of those, 344 were arrested on suspicion of unlawful assembly. It’s unclear how many were charged with a crime.

The department paid about $17.4 million for personnel during the protests, with about $12.2 million going toward overtime.

The LAPD’s actions during the federal immigration operations last year have been widely cited as a source of confusion for city residents who remain uncertain about what police were responsible for during the operations.

The American Civil Liberties Union and other advocacy groups previously reported to the commission about a federal raid at a garment warehouse last June where LAPD set a perimeter for federal agents while they detained workers there. During the presentation, the groups advised that police make it clear to the community in the future what they are there to do.

People echoed during public comment that the same confusion persists in the protest report, which describes the immigration raids and the public response to them as a “complex challenge” for local police.

“The Department’s role was limited to providing public safety support when demonstrations escalated into violence or when federal personnel were at risk of being overwhelmed,” it reads.

For months, immigration advocates and other elected leaders called on McDonnell and Bass to provide more clarity on LAPD’s role in federal immigration sweeps. In February, Bass issued an executive directive explicitly limiting LAPD’s role during these operations and calling for greater transparency about the department's interactions with federal agents.

The death of Jackie, the matriarch of Big Bear’s famous bald eagle nest, has quickly become international news.

People from around the world are mourning Jackie’s loss and remembering her as a fierce protector, a dedicated mother and the bird that inspired thousands to learn more about nature and wildlife.

Tributes are pouring in from individuals and organizations alike, including the San Bernardino County firefighters who kept watch over Jackie as she was waiting for rescue and the L.A. County officials who connected her with care.

TJ Fraser, a resident of Big Bear Valley’s unincorporated community of Fawnskin, described Jackie as a “neighbor” who was a “really important part of this community.”

Fraser said people were deeply pulling for Jackie’s recovery, but as fans come to terms with her death, he’s started to see more hope for the future of the nest and her longtime mate Shadow.

“I think that that's the real great lesson and the takeaway from this,” he said. “Nature adapts, nature always finds balance; that's how it works. And tomorrow is another day.”

State wildlife officials said Jackie’s remains will undergo a necropsy at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance before being transferred to the National Eagle Repository in Colorado.

The repository is a one-of-a-kind facility run by federal wildlife officials. It stores and distributes eagle remains to federally recognized Native American tribes for religious, cultural and ceremonial purposes.

Friends of Big Bear Valley, the nonprofit that launched the popular eagle livestream, said it does not have any input on how Jackie’s remains are handled.

Jackie’s stardom is a big deal

Fraser said his “phone blew up” when Jackie’s death was announced, and the instant reactions of sadness and shock were “overwhelming.”

“It really showed me how much that bird resonated with people around the country and around the world,” he said. “It was truly remarkable.”

But Jackie’s legacy will be intact forever, Fraser said, through the $10 million fundraiser that preserved acres of land near the feathered couple’s nest.

“What she was able to represent brought people to a place of, ‘We want to protect this for them,’” he said. “And that'll never go away.”

Melanie Stagnaro, a resident of L.A.’s Laurel Canyon neighborhood, has been watching Jackie and Shadow for about six years. She said she was stunned by the news of Jackie’s death, but not entirely surprised since Stagnaro thought something may have been wrong with her earlier in the season.

Stagnaro connected with Jackie over motherhood, so she credited her concerns about the eagle's condition to the trials of nesting season.

“I know there's so much more to her, but for me, it was identifying to her as a mom,” Stagnaro said, adding that her kids graduated high school and “left the nest” while Jackie and Shadow’s eaglets were learning to fly and do the same.

With Jackie gone, Stagnaro has started to turn her affection to Shadow, whom she described as a “stud” and a “great dad.”

“He is amazing too, and … I do hope there's another mate for him,” she said. “And I do hope they keep it at this nest, you know?”

State officials and orgs are still mourning

Jackie’s legacy extends beyond the individual impact to institutions and state leaders, including Gov. Gavin Newsom.

“California mourns Jackie, the Big Bear bald eagle who reminded us of the beauty and wonder of California’s wildlife, and our shared responsibility to protect the habitats that sustain it," Newsom said in a statement Tuesday.

Visit Big Bear said Jackie captured the hearts of the mountain community and so many beyond.

“We know you are with Sandy now, watching over Big Bear together,” the group said on social media. Sandy Steers, the late leader of Friends of Big Bear Valley, died in February.

The San Bernardino County Fire Protection District, which kept watch over Jackie while she was waiting for rescuers, said it was inspiring to see the community come together with compassion and concern for her well-being.

The Institute for Wildlife Studies, which helped bald eagles return to Southern California’s Channel Islands, said Jackie became a powerful symbol of resilience, beauty and the importance of protecting wildlife.

“While we mourn her passing, we also reflect with gratitude on the legacy she leaves behind,” the institute said on social media Tuesday. “May Jackie’s story continue to inspire compassion for wildlife, stewardship of natural places, and a commitment to protecting bald eagles and other wild species.”

Support ‘In honor of Jackie’

The Ojai Raptor Center, which gave Jackie intensive care for about three weeks, is still seeing a flood of donations after her death, according to its website.

Around 20,000 people have supported its bald eagle recovery campaign. Thousands of dollars were donated throughout Tuesday and Wednesday, along with messages like, “In honor of Jackie and all you did to save her,” and, “ALL OF YOU ARE HEROES for your dedication & tireless work for Jackie and every animal you care for."

text:
On June 25, 2026, the Supreme Court issued a ruling in Mullin v. Doe that has devastating implications for many people with Temporary Protected Status (TPS). TPS has historically allowed people from specific countries to remain in the US and to work here if it is not safe for them to return home due to war, disasters, or other emergencies.

The ruling allowed the Trump administration to end TPS for Haitians and Syrians, which it has now done. The ruling also largely clears the way for the Trump administration to end TPS for people from other countries, if it chooses to do so.

Click here to see the latest updates about the status of TPS for Afghanistan, Burma (Myanmar), Cameroon, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Honduras, Hong Kong, Lebanon, Liberia, Nepal, Nicaragua, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Yemen.

TPS provides protection against detention and deportation, as well as legal authorization to work. You may have both TPS and some other status.

If you only have TPS, and do not have any other status or a pending application that permits you to remain in the U.S., and your TPS ends, you will be considered to be unlawfully present and removable.

This does not mean that you are likely to be detained or deported from your home or in public, but does significantly increase the risk of detention and deportation from any interaction with immigration authorities. Not all pending applications protect you from being detained or deported.

Being in the U.S. for a period of time (more than six or twelve months) without authorization can bar you from re-entering the U.S. if you leave the country.

Some TPS holders have already accrued “unlawful presence” that would bar re-entry, however, unlawful presence does not hinder you from obtaining certain forms of relief and there are certain exceptions which may apply. Whether you should be concerned about the unlawful presence bar is specific to your situation. It is important that you consult a trusted immigration lawyer.

Being in the U.S. for a period of time (more than six or twelve months) without authorization can bar you from re-entering the U.S. if you leave the country.

Some TPS holders have already accrued “unlawful presence” that would bar re-entry, however, unlawful presence does not hinder you from obtaining certain forms of relief and there are certain exceptions which may apply. Whether you should be concerned about the unlawful presence bar is specific to your situation. It is important that you consult a trusted immigration lawyer.

Congress has the power to pass legislation protecting people from TPS from deportation. In fact, members of the House of Representatives are now attempting to pass the Dream and Promise Act, which would provide many people who have or had TPS with a path to citizenship. There are other bills that address the crisis facing people with TPS, including the SECURE Act, and country specific bills, including a bill extending TPS for Haitians, which passed the House but has yet to be considered in the Senate.

Contact your Congress members to urge them to support the Dream and Promise Act and other protections for people with TPS.

If you have children who would remain in the US without you if you were deported, decide who will care for them and fill out any necessary legal papers with your authorization. These papers may depend on what state the children will live in.

Consider what to do about financial accounts, business interests, bills, and property in the event that you are deported, and leave any necessary instructions to others.

text:
A metro Atlanta congresswoman is co-sponsoring a bill that would stop the Transportation Security Administration from sharing its data with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Rep. Nikema Williams, who is up for reelection in November, announced that she is supporting the No TSA Data for ICE Act, which was introduced by Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib.

If passed, the bill would prevent the TSA from sharing data that includes passenger names and birth dates with ICE. Democratic lawmakers say the communication has led to a surge of arrests at airports across the country, with ICE agents targeting immigrants who are waiting for visa extensions or have employment authorization documentation.

In July, CBS News reported that TSA has been sharing more information about noncitizen travelers with ICE, giving them "tips" or "leads" that could end in arrest, detainment, and deportation. Sources say that the information sharing included details about immigrants who are just suspected of civil immigration violations, such as overstaying their visa.

The bill would also prevent the Department of Homeland Security from retaliating against critics of the Trump administration or ICE by revoking their status in programs like TSA PreCheck and Global Entry.

Twenty-four other members of Congress are co-sponsoring the bill, including Georgia Rep. Henry C. "Hank" Johnson.

"Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the world's busiest and most efficient airport, is the gateway to the world. That's only possible when every traveler has confidence in our aviation system," Williams said in a statement. "The TSA should play no part in Trump's and ICE's terror campaign. It's exploitative, dangerous, and a violation of people's privacy."

text:
Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) is pressing the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for details on the investigation into former DHS official Corey Lewandowski, who was accused of corruption and mismanagement.

In a letter sent Tuesday to newly confirmed DHS Under Secretary for Management Brian Cavanaugh, Hassan sought interim findings and other records from the department’s review.

“The allegations against Mr. Lewandowski, if true, indicate significant corruption, abuse of taxpayer funds, and flagrant conflicts of interest that require Congressional investigation based on a comprehensive record of his tenure at DHS,” Hassan wrote.

The New Hampshire Democrat, who is also a senior member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, opened her investigation into Lewandowski in June after reports raised questions about his involvement in DHS contracting decisions.

Lewandowski, a longtime ally of President Trump, served as a special government employee at the DHS and was a close adviser to former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

Hassan has alleged that Lewandowski used his position to seek compensation from DHS contractors tied to new or renewed contracts and approved consulting contracts for former political associates of his despite them having no previous experience in Homeland Security policy.

Lewandowski also allegedly reviewed contracts worth more than $100,000 before they could receive Noem’s approval under a newly implemented policy, a process Hassan said delayed critical DHS activities.

Earlier this year, House Democrats asked the DHS inspector general to investigate Lewandowski and sought to rescind the $100,000 contract approval policy.

During Cavanaugh’s nomination hearing, he confirmed that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had begun reviewing contracts Lewandowski may have approved in connection with possible self-dealing and “pay-to-pay” schemes, according to Hassan’s letter.

Cavanaugh had pledged to oversee the process and be “open and transparent and accountable” with oversight committees, and Hassan is asking Cavanaugh to make good on that commitment.

“As the chief management officer and senior acquisition official at DHS, you now have responsibility for overseeing DHS procurement activities and ensuring that the Department spends taxpayer dollars lawfully and effectively,” Hassan wrote.

President Trump on Tuesday once again acknowledged the constitutional restrictions against him seeking a third term in office — an idea he has repeatedly floated during his second administration.

“I’d love to run, but the law is very strong,” he told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews after disembarking from Air Force One.

The president added that he is asked this question “by everyone,” pointing to the crowd at the Patriot Games event in Ohio he had just returned from.

“Even tonight, they’re screaming at the event, ‘2028!’ No, everybody wants me to do it, but the law is very strong,” he continued.

Trump has repeatedly teased the idea of running for the presidency again, despite the 22nd Amendment blocking a president from serving more than two terms.

Congressional Republicans have suggested he was not serious about another bid, despite Trump telling NBC News last year that he was “not joking” about this possibility.

During his speech at the makeup White House Correspondents’ Association dinner at the end of July, the president brought up the topic again.

“I won three times. Now, I’m going to do it again,” he said at the time, donning a red “Trump 2028” hat.

Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have been widely floated as top contenders for the Republican ticket in 2028.

Trump told a crowd at a White House event in May that the pair would be a “dream team” but did not specify whom he would like to see at the top of the ticket.

“That does not mean you have my endorsement under any circumstance,” he clarified. “But you know … I think it sounds like presidential candidate and vice presidential candidate.”

text:
As Mainers continue to target Sen. Susan Collins' office with protests following a recent killing by an immigration agent, new reporting shows how some of the $70 billion she and her GOP colleagues gave to President Donald Trump's immigration agencies is being spent.

According to the Associated Press on Tuesday:

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers may soon be outfitted with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks intended to gain compliance from combative individuals.

ICE plans to spend up to $20 million to purchase thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.

The devices are known as the GLOVE, which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky. They have been used in recent years by some jails and police departments.

As the company's website explains, "the discomfort associated with the stimulation is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds and leaves no burns, marks, or scars." It describes them as a "humane, low-optics, de-escalation solution for many situations facing our men and women in uniform."

John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, told the AP that the sensation is "immediate and sharp," comparing it to a "bee sting."

While he said it could be an effective tool to prevent "resistance," he warned that it should not be used as a form of punishment against those merely exhibiting “verbal defiance or belligerence” or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women, or elderly or disabled people.

But given the recent record of rampant civil rights abuses, extrajudicial killings, excessive use of force, and efforts to lie about misconduct, civil rights advocates are warning that these gloves are being placed into, or onto, the exact wrong hands.

"ICE spent the last year showing this country that they are willing to disregard the law and are too quick to use force, with devastating and at times fatal consequences for citizens and noncitizens alike," Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, told Common Dreams. "Now they might be equipped with a device that allows them to deliver an electric shock with their hands by pushing a small button, in a move that might be imperceptible to those watching."

Kica Matos, president of the National Immigration Law Center, concurred, telling Common Dreams that ICE is a "rogue agency with an $80 billion slush fund that allows them to concoct and fund new ways to visit cruelty upon our communities."

"Arming poorly trained agents with electric shock gloves to inflict pain on our neighbors is disgusting and barbaric," Matos added. "Congress must end the blank check to ICE, and ICE must get out of our communities.”

The shock gloves are just one way that immigration agencies are spending the $70 billion in additional funding they were given back in June, when Republicans in the Senate voted 52-47 to authorize the funding despite rampant lawlessness. Only one Republican, Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), voted against supercharging the funding.

In a July 16 letter to Democratic Gov. Janet Mills, Collins defended her vote for the increased ICE funding by pointing to "reforms" passed in April as part of the Department of Homeland Security's broader appropriations bill, which included $20 million for body cameras and $2 million for "de-escalation" training.

Collins' office did not immediately respond when asked by Common Dreams whether she believes electric shock gloves were a good form of "de-escalation."

A five-term senator in the midst of a fierce reelection bid against Democrat Troy Jackson has taken fierce criticism for her vote to support ICE on the campaign trail, which has only grown in intensity since July's fatal shooting of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford.

It was one of two fatal shootings of men without criminal records over the course of a week. ICE later acknowledged that the victims were not the target of their operations.

When asked after the shooting, Collins declined to say that she regretted her vote for increased ICE funding.

Protesters who gathered outside Collins' Biddeford office on Tuesday said she should.

"$70 billion to fund the terror that left my family and community in fear,” Fernanda McLaughlin, a Maine resident and community organizer, said over the loudspeaker, according to NBC News Center Maine. "You know what that money can be really used for? To feed Mainers. To fund our schools. To fund our health system."

"There were no guardrails included, and she still voted yes on it," McLaughlin said. "Simple guardrails that exist in nearly every other law enforcement agency across our nation."

text:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who scored an impressive win in Minnesota's Democratic primary for Senate, wants to blow up Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after two slayings rattled her state earlier this year.

"Now let's talk about Donald Trump's out of control ICE force," Flanagan said during her victory speech Tuesday night. "We need to rip ICE apart and stop them from terrorizing our communities. And I know this. I know that we can fix our broken immigration system, secure the border, and create a real pathway to citizenship that aligns with our values."

Flanagan is another progressive insurgent challenging the status quo in the Democratic Party and handed Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., another defeat in the progressive proxy war in her decisive victory over Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn.

REPUBLICANS GET THE DEMOCRAT THEY WANTED AS SOCIALIST ABDUL EL-SAYED WINS MICHIGAN SENATE PRIMARY

Flanagan, like other progressives in the hunt for a position of power in Congress, has honed her left-leaning bona fides by backing Medicare for all and pushing an end to military aid to Israel.

She’s vowed to go after ICE on the campaign trail in the wake of the two deadly immigration enforcement-related shootings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota, and used Craig’s support of legislation, like the Laken Riley Act, as a political cudgel to build a distinction between the two of them.

Those positions have earned her the backing of progressive heavyweights like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and even Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., whose decision to retire from the Senate opened up the contest.

Notably, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who is running for governor, has not weighed in on the race so far.

Craig, who was viewed as the safer, more moderate pick, had the backing of the Democratic old-guard, including Schumer.

BIG MONEY PROPELS DEM MEGACHURCH PASTOR TO VICTORY IN LONGSHOT KANSAS SENATE BID

Republicans are licking their chops, too, at Schumer getting handed another loss.

"Morale among Chuck Schumer’s establishment is at an all-time low, and Bernie Sanders’ socialist flank is filling the gap with candidates like Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed," Bernadette Breslin, a spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told Fox News Digital.

And it’s also brought reams of cash into the race. Craig has raised nearly $13 million this cycle, according to filings from the Federal Election Commission, while Flanagan has raked in just shy of $7 million.

"Peggy Flanagan is about bringing about real change, standing up to the big money interests," Sanders told "Face the Nation" on Sunday. "There is a reason why the super PACs and the billionaires are flooding Minnesota with all kinds of money. Same thing as Michigan."

Republicans see Flanagan’s candidacy in the same vein as Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who last week similarly squeaked out a narrow win over Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who, like Craig, has Schumer’s backing.

BOMB-THROWER DEM MAKES SHOCKING PROMISE TO KICK SCHUMER TO CURB DURING SENATE DEBATE

They also have built-in messaging against her: Flanagan was Walz’s right hand as the Minnesota fraud scandal rippled across the airwaves and nation. While the scandal killed his prospects of running for reelection as governor, it has so far not kneecapped Flanagan's candidacy. And Walz hasn't waded into the endorsement game in the Senate contest, either.

They’re confident that national Republicans’ candidate of choice, former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, will be the one to turn Minnesota red. There's also the possibility that Flanagan, who has not raked in the same level of cash that Craig did, may become a resource drain for other key races on Democrats' scorecard.

"Minnesota and Michigan being in play was not on Chuck Schumer’s bingo card this cycle," a GOP operative told Fox News Digital. "It remains to be seen which battleground(s) Democrats will have to pull resources from to drag socialists like Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed across the finish line in November."

And Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., when asked by CNN which races kept him up at night, said one contest gave him hope.

"What we know without question is, she is within a point of the lieutenant governor right now," he said. "So if we can continue to let her show the contrast between the two candidates, I think Michele Tafoya's the kind of Republican that can win."

title: In Ohio, Haitians' American dream shatters as ICE prepares to deport them - The Guardian
description:

They were about to embark on the drive south to the Blue Ash facility to help Haitians such as Maler in any way they could.
“When he got that letter [requiring him the come to the Blue Ash facility], he was terrified, he got sick,” Dorsainvil said.

text:
When Monsanto Maler walked out of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Blue Ash, Ohio, at 9.15am on Sunday with an ankle monitor freshly attached to his left leg, he put his hand over his face, burst into tears and fell to the ground.

He had come to the US in June 2023, fleeing gangs in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, where he had been hit over the right side of his head, leaving a large, visible scar.

Grief-stricken and unable to hold himself up, he collapsed on the ground, his dozens of immigration documents, which a moment before had been carefully packed under his arm, strewn across the concrete. His face was full of confusion, his eyes bewildered. His American dream had ended in humiliation and despondency, with a metal box tied around his ankle.

“I feel depressed, physically, mentally. I feel dizzy,” he said through an interpreter.

Four hours earlier, 75 miles (120km) to the north in Springfield, Viles Dorsainvil, who heads the Haitian Support Center, and Pastor Carl Ruby loaded into a sedan on a humid, foggy morning at 5.30am. They were about to embark on the drive south to the Blue Ash facility to help Haitians such as Maler in any way they could.

On the drive, the pair talked about their efforts to help a family from Ruby’s church in Springfield emigrate to Quebec City, one of the thousands of Haitians forced to leave the US due to the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant policies.

“I was helping them pack. The dad had all this patriotic stuff with him,” said Ruby, who knows at least two Haitians from his congregation who have been called to Blue Ash to be fitted with ankle monitors.

“It makes me sad that what he’s going to remember from the United States is that he had to leave.”

Dorsainvil talked about a Haitian man who worked at a local Amazon warehouse, had temporary protected status (TPS) until 2029 and had come to his center last Friday seeking help. “When he got that letter [requiring him the come to the Blue Ash facility], he was terrified, he got sick,” Dorsainvil said.

Dorsainvil, himself a TPS holder, and Ruby chatted about what was happening in Haiti right now – that a burger there cost $16 and how the absence of opportunity was pushing people into gangs or to flee the country for their lives.

On 5 August, the Washington DC district judge Ana Reyes, whose ruling had previously prevented the Trump administration from lifting TPS for hundreds of thousands of Haitians, was forced to remove her stay, following a decision from the supreme court backing the Trump administration’s efforts. It means that for about 350,000 Haitians in the US on TPS, it’s an end for their lives in the US.

Over the last decade, more than 12,000 Haitians moved to the Rust belt town of Springfield, where they worked in labor-intensive jobs in manufacturing and food packaging, jobs that local companies struggled to fill.

But in September 2024, then presidential candidate Donald Trump falsely claimed that immigrants in Springfield were eating pets, setting off a firestorm of unrest that fueled neo-Nazi marches, bomb threats and school closures in Springfield, and the national immigration debate centered on the town of 60,000 people.

In recent weeks, dozens of Haitian nationals living in Springfield – some who had applied for asylum, others who had TPS – have begun receiving emails from the Department of Homeland Security ordering them to show up at the Blue Ash facility, often early on a Sunday morning. The letter, a photo of which was seen by the Guardian, contained no stated reason for the requirement or an indication that a monitoring device would be attached to their bodies.

According to advocates and lawyers representing the Haitian nationals, those who received the ankle monitors will not be allowed to travel more than 75 miles from their home without the consent of an immigration judge. The Blue Ash Ice office is at least 71 miles from Springfield.

By 7am outside the Ice facility, streams of protesters – nuns and priestesses, children, and men wearing USA hockey jerseys – had positioned themselves along the road in front of the building.

Aside from one marked DHS police vehicle parked outside, the ICE building, a single-story, red-brick office, had no obvious marking to indicate its use as a federal government facility.

“Life there is extremely difficult. Haiti is the poorest country in the western hemisphere; [it’s a country] exploited for all of its resources,” said Lorne Hlad, a pastor from Cincinnati attending the protest, who has worked in Haiti and visited six times.

“[TPS] should be renewed. Gangs control Port-au-Prince; there’s no active government. Sending people back to a country that has no infrastructure to protect them is inhumane.”

At 7.40am, the first Haitian national, a man dressed all in black, arrived for his appointment. By 8am three people, including Maler, had arrived. Thirty minutes later, a Haitian man and woman arrived and were given communion by Ruby, who had brought a vat of wine, bread and a large gold cross.

“We want to give them the message that Jesus is with them,” said Ruby.

“The Bible isn’t policy, but the Bible is very clear that God loves immigrants. It teaches that they are to have access to justice.”

Dorsainvil and immigration lawyers said they were assisting Haitians to file a motion for amelioration that could remove or replace the ankle monitors with monitoring devices worn on the wrist.

“The wrist monitors may be slightly less stigmatizing,” said Heather Campbell, an immigration lawyer representing several of the Haitian immigrants.

“But anything that differentiates you from somebody else, especially if you are part of a community that people know this is happening to, it’s going to make you uncomfortable.”

Questions sent by the Guardian both to Ice and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asking, among other things, the stated objective of attaching ankle bracelets to Haitian nationals, were not directly responded to. Instead, Ice shared a statement that read: “Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations.”

Organizers of Sunday’s protest estimate that about 700 people showed up to support the Haitian immigrants.

“It’s reminiscent of the shackles used during slavery, something the Haitian people are very familiar with, after liberating themselves from slavery in the late 18th century,” said Samantha Searl of Ignite Peace, the non-profit leading the protest action outside the Ice facility.

“The ankle monitors send a message to all immigrants that they will always continue to be subjected to the violence of our punitive immigration system.”

Facing midterm elections in November, recent polls show American public opinion is souring on the Trump administration’s Ice enforcement activity. A YouGov poll released on 21 July found that just 30% of those surveyed believe Ice has been using necessary and justified force in its activities.

Having gotten back to his feet and walking a short distance from the Ice facility, Maler, still visibly reeling from what happened to him, was driven away by a friend in a small sedan car, his hopes and dreams of a better life in America shattered.

On the drive back to Springfield, Ruby and Dorsainvil stopped at a McDonald’s. Ruby ordered an iced tea, Dorsainvil some ice water.

Dorsainvil was clearly exhausted – he said he stayed up late the previous night working on his university thesis.

“It’s a study of the economic impact of Haitian immigrants on Springfield,” he said.

text:
Four human rights groups are suing the Trump administration over its economic pressure campaign against the International Criminal Court (ICC), arguing that sanctions against judges, prosecutors and others are unlawfully interfering with their international criminal justice work.

The lawsuit was filed Tuesday in New York by the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch and the Open Society Institute, which claim they have been forced to scale back human rights and legal work because of the administration’s actions.

“The Sanctions Regime has been exceptionally disruptive to the international justice system as a whole and caused serious harm to the global human rights community,” attorneys wrote. “Individuals and organizations, including Plaintiffs, have been forced to cease engaging as they had before with the ICC or the designated individuals and organizations because of the risk of severe civil or criminal penalties, or in the case of non-U.S. citizens, designation for sanctions themselves.”

At the center of the lawsuit is an executive order that President Trump signed last year in February that accused the ICC of engaging in “illegitimate and baseless actions” by pursuing war crimes cases against Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for alleged human rights abuses in Gaza.

It resulted in the State Department issuing sanctions against ICC prosecutors, judges, Palestinian human rights groups and Francesca Albanese, an Italian lawyer who serves as the United Nations special rapporteur for the Palestinian territory.

The complaint argues that this “financial death penalty” has caused “grave damage” to the ICC’s ability to prosecute perpetrators of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

It is the second lawsuit challenging the executive order in as many months. Three of the court’s judges have also sued to block the sanctions against them.

“The fact that so many leading human rights and humanitarian organizations have come together to challenge Trump’s unlawful executive order demonstrates the widespread harm it is causing across civil society groups dedicated to bringing those responsible for grave crimes to justice,” said Andrew Loewenstein of Foley Hoag LLP, the lead counsel on the most recent lawsuit.

“The plaintiffs are seeking an end to this sanctions regime, which transgresses the president’s authority and violates international and US law, including the rights to freedom of expression and religion,” he added.

The Hill has reached out to the State Department for comment.

The U.S. never ratified the Rome Statute, the founding treaty that established the ICC in the early 2000s, and therefore is not party to the tribunal, which is based in The Hague, Netherlands.

Trump has been deeply critical of the ICC, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a diplomatic effort last month to “dismantle” the body, accusing it of posing an “intolerable threat” to U.S. sovereignty.

text:
Immigrant advocates are canvassing Little Haiti to inform Haitian immigrants about their rights as Temporary Protected Status protections end for thousands of people in the five boroughs.

About a dozen volunteers, alongside City Councilwoman Farah Louis and Assemblywoman Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn, visited local businesses to reach people directly affected by the loss of TPS.

The group stopped at hair salons, hardware stores and ice cream shops, sharing information and resources with the community.

“They’re all living in fear, uncertainty. They feel isolated and they feel like they are not wanted by their own municipality,” Louis said.

“This is a sanctuary city and a city like New York should be welcoming immigrants, and they feel that Haitians are singled out. They feel like there wasn’t much resistance to stand up for the Haitian people,” Bichotte Hermelyn said.

For some volunteers, the effort was personal.

“It’s a stressful situation, and so we come out to help people and to support them, to know they are here to stay. And this is their country now,” said Lesley Pierre, a Haitian immigrant and volunteer.

Michaella Blemur, whose parents immigrated from Haiti, said she understands how difficult it can be for immigrant families to navigate life in the United States.

“Both of my parents immigrated from Haiti, and growing up and witnessing all the challenges they had to face — English not being their first language, having an accent, experiencing challenges in the workplace — I know how easy it is to feel helpless,” Blemur said.

The Trump administration earlier this year determined that Haiti no longer met the conditions for TPS, arguing that the federal program was intended to be temporary. The decision was challenged in federal court, but a judge ruled that the protections could be terminated.

The canvass is one of several efforts organized by immigrant advocacy groups, including the New York Immigration Coalition, as Haitian immigrants lose TPS protections and concerns grow over increased Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in New York City.

“We’ve seen what ICE has done across this country, and we know that they are lawless and rogue,” said Murad Awawdeh, president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition.

Awawdeh said there are an estimated 40,000 Haitian TPS holders in New York City. The loss of their status has left many without jobs and uncertain about what comes next.

“They are the nurses in our hospitals. The construction workers who are making sure our homes are being built, repairs are happening. And the Trump administration is just constantly sowing more panic, chaos and fear,” Awawdeh said.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani has been in direct conversations with President Donald Trump about renewing TPS for Haitians or granting them another form of legal status.

text:
FORT WORTH (KXAS)—A North Carolina pastor was detained by U.S. Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) and had a stroke while in custody, according to his family. Now, he's in a Fort Worth area hospital, and they're worried about the medical care he's getting.

ICE said the pastor, 55-year-old Gabriel Johnson, who has been in the U.S. for more than 30 years, was detained nearly a month ago for overstaying his visa. ICE also confirmed he was taken to the hospital on July 30th with stroke symptoms.

His family said in 2004, he was issued a withholding of removal, allowing him to stay in the U.S. Since being hospitalized, they said they have not been able to get much information on how he's doing, as they've only been briefly able to speak with him.

"While our dad was detained his first two weeks, he was able to at least give us phone calls throughout the day, check in with us, and we would check in him," Gabri said. "But now that he's been hospitalized, we have not been allowed regular phone calls or updates on his health status. And it's been somehow even worse than when he was first taken."

Johnson is described by his family as a loving father, husband, brother, and man of strong faith. Now his daughter leads their desperate push to keep his story in the spotlight.

"Please if anyone lives in the state of Texas, or works with immigration law and reform, I will do anything," Gabri Johnson said in a desperate plea in her now-viral social media video she posted after her father was detained by ICE at his home.

"Just please help bring my father back home," Gabri said.

According to Johnson's family, he was brought to a detention facility in Texas where he then had a stroke, after just over two weeks in ICE custody.

ICE told NBC News Johnson, from Liberia, entered the country nearly 40 years ago on a 6-month visa. They say he was ordered to leave 35 years ago.

NBC News reports ICE said Johnson was taken to the hospital with stroke symptoms on July 30, is now stable and has access to 24-hour emergency care. According to ICE, detainees are not allowed to use their cell phones, but are allowed visitation.

"He is not getting the rehabilitation or treatment that he needs," Gabri said. "He has remained on his back in that hospital bed."

The Johnson family, concerned about the medical care he's receiving while in ICE custody, flew to Texas from North Carolina, and said they only briefly got to see him. They said during their visit he was cuffed to his hospital bed.

"We have to fight for the right to have a say in his medical treatment," Gabri said. "We've asked, is ICE making decisions for him? There is a lack of dignity and a serious amount of control."

Johnson's family is now asking questions about the line between federal immigration and local hospitals--as they take legal steps to try to get him released.

"We would like to see my father and thousands of other people treated with respect and dignity toward their basic human rights in the form of healthcare," Gabri said.

ICE told NBC News Johnson will be transferred to a rehab facility and deported once medically cleared, adding that has a criminal history but did not provide any evidence supporting that.

“Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, ICE is targeting the worst of the worst," ICE said in a statement.

According to ICE, nearly 70 percent of ICE arrests involve individuals who are charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S.
